overview: Black–Scholes–Merton prices a European option by constructing, on paper, a portfolio of the underlying and cash that replicates the option's payoff, and arguing that two things with identical payoffs must cost the same. The famous formula is the closed-form solution of that argument under lognormal dynamics. Its deepest practical consequence is that the market quotes options *through* it: traders exchange implied volatilities, not prices, using the model as a common language even where they doubt its assumptions.
formula_latex: C = S e^{-qT} N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2), \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r - q \pm \sigma^2/2)\,T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}

variables.name: Spot price
variables.why_it_matters: The anchor of the replication argument. For a call, value rises roughly delta-for-one with spot; the model's whole machinery describes how that exposure changes as S moves.

variables.name: Strike
variables.why_it_matters: Sets where optionality lives. Far from the strike the option behaves like stock or like nothing; near it, gamma and vega concentrate, which is why the interesting risk sits close to at-the-money.

variables.name: Volatility
variables.why_it_matters: The only input you cannot observe directly, and therefore the one the whole market argues about. Higher volatility widens the distribution of outcomes; since the option keeps the upside and refuses the downside, its value increases in σ — always.

variables.name: Time to expiry
variables.why_it_matters: Time is raw material for volatility to act on: what enters the maths is σ√T, so doubling time is worth less than doubling vol. As T→0 the value collapses to intrinsic.

variables.name: Risk-free rate
variables.why_it_matters: Sets the cost of carrying the replicating portfolio and the discounting of the strike. Calls gain from higher r (you defer paying K), puts lose.

variables.name: Dividend yield
variables.why_it_matters: Cash the holder of the option never receives but the holder of the stock does. It leaks out of the forward: higher q lowers calls and raises puts.

assumptions: The underlying follows geometric Brownian motion: returns are normal, prices lognormal, volatility constant.
Continuous, frictionless hedging — no transaction costs, no jumps you cannot trade through.
Borrowing and lending happen at one constant risk-free rate; dividends accrue continuously at rate q.
European exercise only: the right can be used at expiry, never before.
No arbitrage: the replication argument is what fixes the price.
limitations: The volatility smile is the market rejecting constant σ in public: out-of-the-money puts trade at higher implied vols than the model says they should, because real returns have fat left tails.
Jumps break the hedge. In a gap move the continuous rebalancing story fails precisely when it matters most.
Not valid for American options (early exercise has value, especially puts and calls on dividend payers) or for path-dependent payoffs.
Assumes constant rates — harmless for a 3-month equity option, badly wrong for long-dated or rates-sensitive products.
when_to_use: Vanilla European options on liquid underlyings with short-to-medium maturities; anywhere you need a fast, differentiable price; and always as the quoting convention — converting between price and implied volatility.
when_not_to_use: American-style exercise, strong smile/skew exposure (deep OTM strikes, crash protection), path-dependent exotics, or long-dated options where stochastic rates and vol matter. Reach for trees (early exercise), local/stochastic vol (smile), or Monte Carlo (path dependence) instead.
industry_usage: The lingua franca of option markets: quotation in implied vol, first-cut risk (the Greeks), and the baseline every fancier model is benchmarked against.
computational_complexity: O(1) — a closed form; prices and all first-order Greeks cost microseconds.
comparison_note: The closed form is the reference point: exact within its own assumptions, instant, and deterministic. When the tree or Monte Carlo disagree with it here, the gap is *numerical* (discretization or sampling), not economic — all three share the same lognormal world.
